art.text: Across the Neolithic and Bronze Age, people in Ireland and Britain carved rock art. Most of it is abstract, usually cup and ring marks, though spirals and figurative depictions of weaponry are also known. This tradition connected with others along Atlantic Europe, particularly in Galicia.
art.source_title: Neolithic and Bronze Age rock art in the British Isles

art.text: Surviving rock art in Ireland and the British Isles is believed to be only a small sample of what was made. Many carvings would have eroded away. Other images might have been painted onto rock or marked onto wood, livestock or the human body, and so failed to survive.
art.source_title: Neolithic and Bronze Age rock art in the British Isles

art.text: Britain was the first region in Europe to fully adopt tin-bronze technology. It switched all its metalwork from copper and arsenical bronze to full tin-bronze in the period 2200-2100 BC. This later spread across Scandinavia and Central Europe by around 1800 BC.

The Atlantic Bronze Age was marked by distinct regional centers of metal production linked by regular maritime trade. The main centers were in southern England and Ireland, northwestern France, and western Iberia. Items from this culture are often found in hoards or ritual deposits.

Archaeologists know of three instances in South West Britain where weapons were carved into stone. They appear at Boscawen-un stone circle in Cornwall, Badbury Rings Barrow in Dorset, and Stonehenge in Wiltshire. The Boscawen-un weapons are tentatively dated to circa 2000 BCE, the others to c. 1800 BCE.
art.source_title: Neolithic and Bronze Age rock art in the British Isles

art.text: Within Britain, most recorded Neolithic and Bronze Age rock art comes from the northern part of the island, where cup-and-ring marks are particularly common. Over 70 examples have been found in the South West, far fewer. Rock art specialist George Nash considered the South West petroglyphs a distinct artistic tradition from the North.
art.source_title: Neolithic and Bronze Age rock art in the British Isles

art.text: Metalwork of the Atlantic Bronze Age included socketed and double-ring bronze axes, sometimes buried in large hoards in Brittany and Galicia. Military equipment such as lunate spearheads, V-notched shields and carp-tongue swords is usually found buried in lakes, rivers or rocky outcrops.

Elite feasting equipment such as spits, kettles and meat hooks has been found from central Portugal to Scotland. Metal finds from this culture have typically been preserved in watery contexts such as rivers, lakes and bogs.

Rock art specialist study of the carvings' purpose has produced no agreement. Amateur researcher Ronald Morris listed 104 different proposals that he had encountered for the purposes of the petroglyphs, ranking them by what he believed to be their plausibility.
art.source_title: Neolithic and Bronze Age rock art in the British Isles

art.text: Recent tooth enamel isotope research on bodies in early Bronze Age graves around Stonehenge indicates that at least some immigrants came from the area of modern Switzerland. The Beaker people brought metalworking in copper and gold from 2500 BC, and by 2200 BC had begun producing tin-bronze.

In Britain, rock art had ceased by the time of the agricultural intensification in the Late Bronze Age, in the first millennium BCE. The South West's harder plutonic granite may partly explain why fewer carvings survive there than in the North.
art.source_title: Neolithic and Bronze Age rock art in the British Isles

science.text: Cornwall and Devon hold the largest tin reserves in Europe, among the largest in the world. South West England has the earliest evidence for tin ore exploitation in Europe. Southwestern Britain became a major source of tin for the mainland.

Bronze Age metalwork in the Atlantic zone was made at distinct regional centers linked by regular maritime trade. The main centers were southern England and Ireland, northwestern France, and western Iberia. Metal finds are often preserved in watery contexts such as rivers, lakes and bogs.

Britain was the first region in Europe to fully switch its metalwork to tin-bronze, in the period 2200-2100 BC. Scandinavia and Central Europe followed by around 1800 BC. Southern Iberia, the Aegean and Egypt made the switch later, by around 1500/1300 BC.

Britain's Bronze Age metalworking is linked to the arrival of the Bell Beaker culture. Alongside it came a massive genetic shift, with about 90% of Britain's gene pool replaced between 2400 BC and 2000 BC. People with Early European Farmer ancestry were mostly replaced by people with Western Steppe Herder ancestry.

Ireland's Bronze Age began in the centuries around 2000 BC, when copper was alloyed with tin to make Ballybeg type flat axes. The earlier Copper Age had produced flat axes, daggers, halberds and awls in copper. The rich copper ores of Tipperary, Kerry and west Cork supplied the raw material.

In Cornwall, Middle Bronze Age settlements grew much more numerous and consisted of substantial roundhouses. Monument construction declined while livestock and arable farming expanded. This contrasts with the Early Bronze Age, when the few known domestic buildings were fragile and temporary.

Britain was the first region in Europe to switch all its metalwork to full tin-bronze, in the period 2200-2100 BC. Its tin came from what is now Cornwall and Devon, the largest reserves in Europe, and full tin-bronze use later spread across Central Europe by around 1800 BC.

Isotope analysis shows that some people buried near Stonehenge came from far away. The Amesbury Archer, a metal worker from 2300 BC, grew up near the Alpine foothills of Germany, and the Boscombe Bowmen probably arrived from Wales or Brittany, France. A teenage boy buried about 1550 BC was raised near the Mediterranean Sea.

Stonehenge shows close similarities to the Pömmelte circular enclosure in central Germany, built by Bell Beaker people around 2300 BC. Woodhenge, near Stonehenge, was a large timber circle dated to the early Beaker period or just before. Some researchers suggest it may have been a monumental roofed building.

politics.text: Archaeologist Stuart Piggott, who defined the Wessex culture in 1938, described it as an underlying substratum overlaid by an intrusive ruling class. This ruling class opened trading networks with France and central and northern Europe. It imported bronze tools and probably also artisans.

In Lower Brittany, the Armorican Tumulus culture left more than a thousand Bronze Age burial sites. Many are exceptionally richly endowed burials of chieftains. These were contemporary with the elite of the Wessex culture in England and the Únětice culture in Central Europe.

The wealth from trade probably allowed the Wessex people to build the second and third, megalithic, phases of Stonehenge. It also indicates a powerful form of social organisation. River transport may have made Wessex the main link to the Severn estuary.

The Armorican Tumulus culture was a hierarchical society. Its burial mounds were grouped in classic clusters, similar to those of the Wessex culture in Britain and the Hilversum culture in Belgium. Settlements had large houses, and status symbols included daggers, halberds and axes.

A golden hat found at Avanton in France dates from the late Tumulus period, around 1400 BC. Researchers think it may have been worn by elite religious figures, described as 'oracles' or 'king-priests'. Its patterns are thought to represent calendars, like those on the Schifferstadt hat in Germany.

Ross Island was the sole source of copper in Ireland between 2500 and 2200 BCE. Two thirds of copper artefacts from Britain show the same signature, so Irish copper was a major export. It makes up 12% of analysed copper artefacts in the Netherlands and 6% in Brittany.

The Wessex culture had links to the Armorican Tumulus culture in northern France, the Únětice culture in central Germany, and even Mycenaean Greece. It is divided into Wessex I (2000 to 1650 BC) and Wessex II (1650 to 1400). Piggott attributed its origin to an 'actual ethnic movement' from Northern France.

philosophy.text: Stonehenge was built in several phases, beginning about 3100 BC and continuing until about 1600 BC. The ruined monument is aligned towards the sunrise on the summer solstice and the sunset on the winter solstice. Proposed functions include an astronomical observatory or a religious site.

Seahenge was a timber circle with an upturned tree root at its centre, built in Norfolk in the spring-summer of 2049 BC. The current theory is that it and the nearby Holme II were used for ritual purposes, and Holme II in particular has been interpreted as a mortuary monument that may once have formed the boundary of a burial mound. Some have also suggested Seahenge was a site of excarnation, a "sky burial" where the dead were left out to be stripped of flesh, though there is no direct evidence for this.

The Calanais Stones on the Isle of Lewis were erected around 2750 BC, according to Historic Environment Scotland. Several other circles and alignments lie nearby, which suggests Calanais was an active focus for prehistoric religious activity for at least 1,500 years.

Newgrange, a passage tomb built around 3100 BC in County Meath, is aligned so that the rising sun on the winter solstice shines through a roofbox and floods the inner chamber. There is no agreement on its purpose, but it is believed to have had religious significance.

Timothy Darvill and Geoffrey Wainwright have suggested that Stonehenge was a place of healing, the primeval equivalent of Lourdes. They argue this explains the many burials in the area and the trauma deformity in some graves. They concede the site was probably multifunctional and also used for ancestor worship.

Holme II is a larger ring of two concentric timber circles around a hurdle-lined pit holding two oak logs, and it has been interpreted as a mortuary monument. One suggestion is that the upturned roots of Seahenge were used for excarnation, in which dead bodies were left out so the flesh could be stripped away, and that the remains were later buried in Holme II, which may have held a burial mound, now washed away, reaching to the inner timber circle.

The archaeologist O'Kelly called Newgrange, Knowth and Dowth "the cathedrals of the megalithic religion". He believed hundreds of Irish passage tombs showed a religion that venerated the dead, a "cult of the dead", while other megalithic monuments showed solar-oriented beliefs.

Two similar discs have been found in Ireland: the Lattoon gold disc and the bronze Cooke disc, the latter dated to c. 1500–1300 BC. The Cooke disc has fittings like the Trundholm chariot, suggesting it was once connected to a sun horse and mounted on wheels.

After the Calanais stone circle was set up between 2900 and 2600 BC, a small chambered tomb was inserted into its eastern part. Pottery fragments show it was used for several centuries, including sherds of beaker vessels dating to around 2000 to 1700 BC and sherds of grooved ware.

Some interpret the Newgrange chamber as ritual, capturing the sun's rays on the winter solstice, perhaps signalling that the days would start to get longer again. Alignments found at Knowth, Dowth and the Lough Crew Cairns have led to these monuments being read as calendrical or astronomical devices.

The press named Seahenge in 1998 after the more famous Stonehenge. When it was excavated in 1999, locals wanted it left as a tourist site, while Neopagans protested that removing it insulted the religious beliefs of its original builders.

culture.text: During the British Bronze Age, large megalithic monuments similar to those of the Late Neolithic continued to be built or modified. Sites include Avebury, Stonehenge and Silbury Hill. This has been described as a time when elaborate ceremonial practices emerged among some communities of subsistence agriculturalists of western Europe.

Around 2500 BC a new pottery style arrived in Great Britain with the Bell Beaker culture. Beaker pottery appears alongside flat axes and the burial practice of inhumation. The Bell Beaker culture is associated with the beginning of bronze metalworking in Britain.

From around 1300 BC, Atlantic coastal communities shared a strikingly similar way of life. They stretched from central Portugal through the Atlantic coast of France, including Brittany, to Cornwall and Scotland. Shared traits included cliff castles, stone chevaux-de-frise and domestic architecture, sometimes in the form of roundhouses.

Golden hats from Avanton in France and Schifferstadt in Germany date from about 1400 BC. Researchers think they may have been worn by elite religious figures, described as oracles or king-priests. The patterns on the hats are thought to represent calendars.

A 2018 archaeogenetics study linked the spread of the Bell Beaker culture to Britain with a massive genetic shift. About 90% of Britain's gene pool was replaced within a few hundred years, from 2400 BC to 2000 BC. The authors said this population turnover might be linked with the spread of Celtic language to Britain.

Elite feasting equipment such as spits, kettles and meat hooks has been found from central Portugal to Scotland. Such finds hint at shared feasting customs among the elites of Atlantic communities linked by regular maritime trade.

Atlantic Bronze Age metal items are often found in hoards or in ritual areas. Finds were typically preserved in watery places such as rivers, lakes and bogs. Swords, spearheads and shields are usually found buried in lakes, rivers or rocky outcrops, and large hoards of axes were buried in Brittany.

The Bronze Age in Ireland began in the centuries around 2000 BC, when copper was alloyed with tin to make Ballybeg type flat axes. Rich copper ores in Tipperary, Kerry and west Cork provided the raw material. Ireland is also known for a relatively large number of Early Bronze Age burials.

Tooth enamel isotope research on bodies found in early Bronze Age graves around Stonehenge indicates that at least some of the new arrivals came from the area of modern Switzerland. The Beaker people also introduced practices new to Britain: mummification, burial in log coffins and cranial deformation. They also moved from communal Neolithic burials toward burying individuals, often with a beaker alongside the body.

People of the Beaker period built Seahenge, along with the later phases of Stonehenge. Silbury Hill was also built in the early Beaker period. The Mount Pleasant Phase, dated 2700 to 2000 BC, is when Beaker pottery first appears.
Evolutionary geneticist Ian Barnes said that after the Beaker spread, Britain had a population that for the first time had ancestry and skin and eye pigmentation similar to Britons today.

The patterns on the Avanton and Schifferstadt hats are thought to represent calendars, as on the later and more elaborate Berlin Gold Hat. That hat may encode knowledge of the luni-solar Metonic cycle. Some researchers have suggested that a Venus calendar is encoded on the Schifferstadt hat.
